Both versions use their own big-number addition, so large N won't overflow. I deleted the test binaries afterwards, so `main.rs` is the only file left in the folder.

**How it works:** the two compilers treat a backslash at the end of a `//` comment differently. In C++, a line ending in `// \` carries the comment onto the next line. Rust has no such rule, so the comment stops at the end of the line.

```
// \
/*          <- C++: still part of the comment above. Rust: opens a block comment.
#if 0       <- C++: skip everything until #endif. Rust: inside the comment.
// */       <- Rust: the block comment ends here. C++: an ordinary line comment.
...Rust code...   (C++ skips it because of #if 0)
// \
/*          <- Rust: opens a block comment. C++: still part of the comment above.
#endif      <- C++: stop skipping.
...C++ code...    (Rust sees it as a comment)
// */       <- Rust: the block comment ends here.
```

If you edit the file, keep two rules or one of the compilers will break:
- The Rust section can't contain apostrophes (like `'a` lifetimes or `'x'` char literals), because C++ still reads that text inside the `#if 0` block.
- The C++ section can't contain `/*` or `*/`, because that would end the Rust block comment early.

`g++ -Wall` may also warn about a "multi-line comment"; that's expected and harmless.
